subtopic_detail: Abdominal symptoms in a patient established on clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for three years with good symptom control. He tells you he has not opened his bowels for nine days and has vomited twice today.

His abdomen is distended and tympanic with sluggish bowel sounds and generalised discomfort but no guarding. He mentions he stopped taking his laxative several months ago because he disliked the taste. He has no fever, no cough and no urinary symptoms. His last full blood count two weeks ago showed a neutrophil count within the normal range, and he has had no missed doses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 5.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein 22 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold clozapine and arrange urgent full blood count to exclude neutropenia
options.rationale: His neutrophil count is normal and haematological monitoring is up to date, so agranulocytosis does not explain abdominal distension and vomiting. Withholding clozapine for more than 48 hours also forces a slow retitration with risk of psychotic relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography and troponin testing to assess for myocarditis
options.rationale: Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs characteristically within the first four to eight weeks of treatment and presents with tachycardia, fever and chest symptoms rather than nine days of constipation with distension. It remains an important complication but the timing and presentation do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a stimulant laxative and reassess his bowel function in 48 hours on the ward
options.rationale: Oral laxatives alone are inadequate once obstruction is suspected, and stimulant agents can precipitate perforation in a distended atonic bowel. Laxatives are the mainstay of prevention and of treating uncomplicated constipation, not of suspected ileus. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe an antiemetic and increase his oral fluid intake with a review the following morning
options.rationale: Symptomatic treatment delays recognition of a condition with a case fatality far exceeding that of agranulocytosis, and many antiemetics further slow gut transit. Antiemetics are appropriate once obstruction has been excluded. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal imaging and surgical review for suspected bowel obstruction
options.rationale: Nine days without bowel action, vomiting and a distended tympanic abdomen in a patient on clozapine indicates gastrointestinal hypomotility progressing towards ileus, which carries a mortality substantially higher than agranulocytosis and demands urgent imaging and surgical assessment. Recognising it requires actively asking about bowels, since patients rarely volunteer the symptom. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Clozapine remains the only agent with established efficacy in treatment resistant schizophrenia, and its monitoring programme is built around agranulocytosis, yet gastrointestinal hypomotility is both more common and more lethal. The drug has potent anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effects on the gut, slowing colonic transit in the majority of patients and producing a spectrum that runs from constipation through faecal impaction to paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon, ischaemia and perforation. Case fatality once ileus develops is high, and deaths substantially outnumber those from agranulocytosis. Patients frequently do not report the symptom, partly through negative symptoms and reduced interoceptive awareness, so bowel function must be asked about at every review rather than waiting for a complaint. Prophylactic laxatives are recommended for all patients on clozapine, and constipating co-prescriptions such as anticholinergics and opioids should be avoided or minimised.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis
Patients under-report bowel symptoms, so ask directly at every review
Myocarditis typically occurs in the first four to eight weeks, not after years of stable therapy
Prophylactic laxatives are recommended for all patients taking clozapine
Suspected ileus needs imaging and surgical review, not further oral laxatives
explanation.pearls: Avoid adding anticholinergic agents such as benztropine to a patient on clozapine, since the combined gut slowing is a recognised precipitant of ileus, and prescribe a regular osmotic laxative from initiation rather than waiting for constipation to be reported.

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural and mood change after commencing high dose corticosteroid
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 54 year old woman on the respiratory ward. She was admitted six days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation and started on prednisolone 50 mg daily. Over the past three days she has slept only two to three hours nightly, talks rapidly and has been ordering expensive items online.

Nursing staff report she is irritable when interrupted and has been telling other patients she has been chosen to reform the hospital. She has no personal or family history of mood disorder and has never had a similar episode. She takes salbutamol and a preventer inhaler, and is on no antibiotics. She is fully oriented with no fluctuation in attention and no visual hallucinations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 136/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), calcium corrected 2.36 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence lithium and arrange level monitoring for a first presentation of bipolar disorder
options.rationale: A mood stabiliser committing her to long term therapy and monitoring is not justified when a clear pharmacological precipitant is present and the syndrome typically resolves with dose reduction. Lithium would be considered if manic episodes recurred independent of steroid exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss reducing the corticosteroid dose with the treating team and start an antipsychotic
options.rationale: The temporal link to high dose corticosteroid with no prior mood history identifies a substance induced mood disturbance, so the priority is to reduce the causative exposure as far as her asthma safely allows while a short course of an antipsychotic controls the acute symptoms. Most cases resolve within days to weeks of dose reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the corticosteroid abruptly today and observe her mental state over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after six days of high dose therapy risks both loss of asthma control and adrenal insufficiency if her exposure is longer than documented. The correct approach is the fastest safe reduction negotiated with the respiratory team, not immediate withdrawal. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant given the disturbed sleep and marked change in her behaviour
options.rationale: Her presentation is elevated and expansive rather than depressed, and an antidepressant would risk worsening the elevated mood state. Antidepressants have a place in the depressive form of steroid induced mood disturbance, which is actually more common overall. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Treat as hyperactive delirium with regular haloperidol and full delirium precautions
options.rationale: Delirium requires disturbed attention and awareness with a fluctuating course, and she is fully oriented with stable attention and no perceptual disturbance. The near-pair distinction rests on attention and fluctuation, which are the defining features of delirium and are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced neuropsychiatric effects are common, dose dependent and frequently misattributed to a primary psychiatric disorder, particularly when a patient has no prior history. Risk rises steeply above the equivalent of 40 mg of prednisolone daily, and symptoms typically emerge within the first two weeks of treatment. The presentations span elevated mood, irritability and psychosis at higher doses, depression which is more common with prolonged therapy, and cognitive disturbance, with a prior psychiatric history a much weaker predictor than is often assumed. Management centres on reducing the corticosteroid to the lowest dose that controls the underlying disease, in negotiation with the treating team rather than unilaterally, since abrupt cessation risks both disease flare and adrenal insufficiency. Symptomatic treatment uses an antipsychotic for elevated or psychotic presentations and an antidepressant for depressive ones, and most episodes resolve within days to weeks of dose reduction.
key_points: Risk rises steeply above the equivalent of 40 mg of prednisolone daily
Symptoms usually appear within the first two weeks of treatment
Elevated and psychotic presentations predominate acutely; depression predominates with prolonged use
Delirium is excluded by preserved attention and the absence of a fluctuating course
Reduce the dose in negotiation with the treating team rather than stopping abruptly
explanation.pearls: Document the reaction prominently, because recurrence on re-exposure is common and a patient who has had steroid induced mania may warrant prophylactic antipsychotic cover if a future high dose course is unavoidable.

subtopic_detail: Weighing antipsychotic risk against harm in dementia related agitation
stem:
You are the visiting medical officer at a residential aged care facility asked to review an 84 year old man with moderate Alzheimer disease. Over three weeks he has become increasingly agitated in the late afternoon, calling out and pushing staff away during personal care, and last week he struck a carer.

Staff have tried moving him to a quieter area without benefit. He has been checked for constipation, urinary retention and infection, all of which were absent, and a hearing aid battery was replaced two weeks ago. His pain is difficult to assess but he has severe knee osteoarthritis and is on no regular analgesia. He is not distressed at other times of day, his attention is stable and there is no acute cognitive fluctuation.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and C-reactive protein within normal limits; midstream urine culture shows no growth; no new medicines in the past three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence regular risperidone at a low dose with review of benefit at 12 weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic may eventually be justified but not before untreated pain has been addressed, and a 12 week review is far too long given the stroke and mortality risk. Where an antipsychotic is used, review is recommended at around four to 12 weeks with an explicit plan to withdraw. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence regular scheduled paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after two weeks
options.rationale: Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible drivers of agitation in dementia, personal care and movement are exactly when osteoarthritic pain is provoked, and he receives no analgesia despite severe knee disease. A trial of regular simple analgesia is low risk and has good evidence for reducing agitation before any antipsychotic is considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a benzodiazepine at night to reduce his arousal and improve his sleep pattern
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines increase falls, confusion and paradoxical agitation in this population and do not address the daytime trigger. They are reserved for short term use in acute severe distress where other measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor to improve cognition and thereby reduce his agitation
options.rationale: These agents produce modest cognitive benefit but have little effect on established agitation and take months to show any change. They are indicated for cognitive symptoms rather than as a behavioural intervention. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant given that late day distress may indicate an underlying depression
options.rationale: Depression is worth considering in dementia but his distress is confined to personal care and movement rather than being pervasive, which points to a pain trigger. An antidepressant trial would be reasonable if there were persistent low mood, tearfulness or withdrawal across the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are best approached as communication of an unmet need rather than as a target for sedation, and a structured search for precipitants precedes any medication decision. The standard sequence examines physical causes including pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sensory impairment and medication effects, then environmental and interpersonal triggers such as noise, overstimulation, unfamiliar carers and the manner in which personal care is delivered. Pain is the most frequently missed contributor because people with moderate to severe dementia cannot report it reliably, and observational pain scales or an empirical trial of regular simple analgesia are the practical responses. Antipsychotics carry a clear increase in stroke and all cause mortality in older people with dementia, so they are reserved for severe distress or risk after non-pharmacological measures have failed, used at the lowest effective dose with informed consent from the substitute decision maker and a defined plan for withdrawal. Australian aged care regulation requires documented justification and review of any psychotropic used for behaviour.
key_points: Treat behaviour as an unmet need and search systematically for precipitants first
Pain is the most commonly missed driver because self report is unreliable in dementia
Agitation confined to personal care and movement points strongly to a pain trigger
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk and require consent and a withdrawal plan
Benzodiazepines worsen falls and confusion and can cause paradoxical agitation
explanation.pearls: A trial of regular scheduled paracetamol, rather than as required dosing, is the single highest yield intervention for agitation in moderate dementia, and benefit should be assessed over about two weeks before escalating to any psychotropic.

subtopic_detail: Persistent sleepiness and low mood in a rotating shift worker
stem:
A 29 year old process operator attends your practice reporting eight months of exhaustion, difficulty concentrating and irritability. He works a rotating roster of four night shifts, then four days off, then four day shifts, and has done so since starting the job.

He says he sleeps only three to four hours after night shifts because of daylight and household noise, and sleeps well for eight hours on his days off, waking refreshed. He enjoys his weekends with friends and denies anhedonia, guilt, hopelessness and suicidal thoughts, and says he feels normal by his third day off. He drinks four cups of coffee during each night shift. He does not snore and his partner has noticed no pauses in his breathing.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and HbA1c all within normal limits; body mass index 24 kg/m2; sleep diary confirms 3 to 4 hours of daytime sleep on night shift blocks and 8 hours on days off

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?

options.text: Shift work disorder from misalignment between his roster and his circadian rhythm
options.rationale: Sleepiness and mood symptoms that track his roster and resolve completely on days off, with normal restorative sleep when he can follow his own rhythm, define a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder rather than a primary psychiatric or medical illness. The complete recovery within days off is the finding that separates it from a depressive episode. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.text: Major depressive disorder presenting predominantly with fatigue and poor concentration
options.rationale: A depressive episode requires persistently low mood or anhedonia for most of the day nearly every day, and his symptoms remit entirely on days off with preserved enjoyment and no guilt or hopelessness. Fatigue alone is insufficient for the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnoea causing fragmented sleep and consequent daytime impairment
options.rationale: He has no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas and a normal body mass index, and his sleep on days off is restorative, which argues against a breathing related disorder. Sleep study referral would be indicated if any of those features were present. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.text: Chronic insomnia disorder maintained by conditioned arousal and poor sleep habits
options.rationale: Chronic insomnia requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity, and his problem is inadequate opportunity because he is trying to sleep in daylight against his circadian drive. He sleeps normally when the opportunity aligns with his rhythm. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.text: Caffeine use disorder producing rebound fatigue and irritability between shift blocks
options.rationale: His intake is substantial and worth addressing, particularly its timing late in a night shift, but caffeine does not account for eight months of sleepiness that resolves entirely on days off. Withdrawal symptoms would be expected on days off when intake falls, which is when he feels best. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

explanation.summary: Shift work disorder is a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder in which the work schedule conflicts with the endogenous circadian drive, producing insomnia during the designated sleep period, excessive sleepiness during work, and consequent mood and cognitive symptoms. Around one in five to one in three shift workers meet criteria, and the diagnosis is frequently mislabelled as depression because fatigue, irritability and poor concentration dominate the presentation. The discriminating feature is that symptoms track the roster and resolve when the worker can sleep according to their own rhythm, whereas a depressive episode persists across days off with anhedonia and negative cognitions. A sleep diary over two weeks is the key diagnostic tool and also exposes the inadequate sleep opportunity that patients often normalise. Management combines sleep hygiene adapted to shift work, strategic light exposure and avoidance, planned napping, careful caffeine timing and forward rotating rosters, with the occupational stakes real because drowsy driving after night shift is a major cause of vehicle crashes.
key_points: Symptoms that resolve completely on days off point to circadian misalignment, not depression
A two week sleep diary is the central diagnostic tool
Chronic insomnia requires adequate sleep opportunity, which shift workers often lack
Forward rotating rosters are better tolerated than backward rotating ones
Drowsy driving after night shift is a major occupational safety risk
explanation.pearls: Advise wearing dark sunglasses on the drive home after a night shift and blocking daylight in the bedroom, since morning light exposure resets the circadian clock in the wrong direction and undoes the day sleep he is trying to obtain.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

subtopic_detail: New low mood in the menopausal transition with vasomotor symptoms
stem:
A 49 year old woman attends your clinic with five months of low mood, poor concentration and loss of interest in activities she previously enjoyed. Her periods have become irregular over the past year, with two gaps of more than 60 days.

She has 10 to 12 hot flushes daily and wakes drenched most nights, which she says is the worst part. She has never had a depressive episode before and has no history of postnatal depression or premenstrual mood change. She denies suicidal thoughts, has no alcohol or drug use, and thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no migraine with aura and no history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-300), HbA1c within normal limits; body mass index 26 kg/m2

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor as first line treatment for the mood symptoms
options.rationale: Antidepressants are first line for a major depressive episode but treat the vasomotor symptoms less effectively than hormonal therapy, and here the flushes and night sweats are driving the sleep disruption that sustains the mood disturbance. They become the preferred choice when hormone therapy is contraindicated or declined. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol to confirm the menopausal transition first
options.rationale: Hormone levels fluctuate widely during the transition and are not recommended for diagnosis in a woman over 45 with typical symptoms and menstrual change. Testing would delay treatment without changing the management decision. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.text: Commence menopausal hormone therapy and review both mood and vasomotor symptoms at six weeks
options.rationale: Where new depressive symptoms arise in the perimenopause alongside prominent vasomotor symptoms and no prior mood history, hormone therapy improves both the flushes and the mood and is the appropriate first recommendation in a woman with no contraindications. Reviewing at six weeks allows an antidepressant to be added if mood does not follow the vasomotor response. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone and review her mood symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a valuable component and helps the distress associated with flushes, but used alone it leaves the nightly vasomotor sleep disruption untreated. It is a reasonable primary choice when a woman declines or cannot take pharmacological treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Recommend a phytoestrogen supplement and lifestyle modification with review in three months
options.rationale: Complementary preparations have inconsistent evidence and do not reliably control moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms or depressive symptoms, so three months of waiting has a substantial opportunity cost. They may suit women with mild symptoms who prefer non-prescription options. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

explanation.summary: The menopausal transition carries a genuinely increased risk of depressive symptoms and of a first depressive episode, with the vulnerability concentrated in the perimenopause rather than after the final menstrual period, and it is greatest in women with a history of premenstrual mood change, postnatal depression or previous depression. Distinguishing a depressive episode arising in this context from one occurring independently matters because the treatment differs: where prominent vasomotor symptoms are disrupting sleep and driving the mood change, hormone therapy improves both, whereas an established major depressive episode with prior history is treated with standard antidepressant and psychological therapy. Diagnosis of the transition itself is clinical in women over 45, and hormone measurement is explicitly not recommended because levels fluctuate unpredictably. Hormone therapy also requires assessment of contraindications including hormone sensitive cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, active liver disease and prior venous thromboembolism, and transdermal preparations carry lower thrombotic risk than oral ones. Where mood does not improve as flushes settle, an antidepressant is added rather than substituted.
key_points: Perimenopause carries greater depressive risk than the postmenopausal years
Prior premenstrual, postnatal or major depression identifies the highest risk group
Hormone measurement is not recommended for diagnosis in women over 45 with typical symptoms
Hormone therapy treats both vasomotor symptoms and associated mood disturbance
Add an antidepressant if mood fails to improve once vasomotor symptoms are controlled
explanation.pearls: Transdermal oestrogen avoids first pass hepatic metabolism and does not carry the increased venous thromboembolism risk seen with oral preparations, making it the preferred route in women with raised body mass index or other thrombotic risk factors.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood
